lecture_context.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models

unit.name: Threat models for modern AI systems
unit.description: Frames the lecture around adversarial robustness and generative modeling, then classifies adversarial attacks into adversarial pixels, data poisoning/backdoors, and prompt injection.
unit.summary: The lecture opens by motivating adversarial robustness as AI models become widely deployed and therefore more exposed to attacks [ts=43s]. It distinguishes the day’s two major topics, adversarial robustness and generative modeling, and notes that the generative part will emphasize GANs and diffusion models [ts=116s]. The adversarial section begins with examples from students and then organizes the field into three waves: imperceptible image perturbations, backdoor/data poisoning attacks from scraped data, and prompt injection or jailbreaking for LLMs [ts=315s]. The instructor emphasizes that new AI agents create extra attack surfaces through instructions, context, and retrieval pipelines, not only raw inputs [ts=464s].

key_points.text: Adversarial robustness matters more as AI models are deployed broadly and become attack targets.
The lecture focuses on adversarial robustness first, then generative models including GANs and diffusion models.
Adversarial examples are described as optical illusions for neural networks caused by small perturbations that change model outputs.
Modern attacks extend beyond inputs to instructions, context, and retrieval pipelines.

kp_catalog.name: AI attack taxonomy
kp_catalog.description: Three-part taxonomy of AI attacks covering adversarial perturbations, data poisoning/backdoors, and prompt injection, with modern attacks expanding to instructions, context, and retrieval.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The instructor explicitly groups attacks into waves and says models now expose more entry points through instructions, context, and retrieval pipelines [ts=315s][ts=464s].
